On this page

Package Manager ​

safeguard is the official SafeC package manager and build system. It is a standalone C++17 binary with no runtime dependencies beyond a working safec compiler and clang linker.

Commands ​

CommandDescription
safeguard new <name> [--lang L] [--std]Scaffold a new project directory with Package.toml and src/main.sc (or, with --lang c/cpp/objc/objcpp, a C, C++ or Objective-C package)
safeguard init [--lang L] [--std]Initialize a Package.toml in the current directory
safeguard fetchClone the git dependencies listed in Package.toml and build the ones from source
safeguard build [--release]Compile the project and all dependencies
safeguard checkFast compile-only pass — reports errors without assembling objects or linking
safeguard std-modules [std/x.h|file...]List the std sources a build compiles and the system libraries it links for them (see Standard Library Modules)
safeguard std-prebuilt <prefix>Compile std for this machine into <prefix>/lib/<triple>/std/<section>.a, one archive per section: the prebuilt std a release ships
safeguard testBuild and run every file under tests/ as an independent binary
safeguard runBuild and execute the project binary
safeguard bundle [--sign <identity>]Build the binary and package it as an application: .app, app folder or .deb (see App Bundles)
safeguard cleanRemove the build/ directory and all artifacts
safeguard verify-lockCheck Package.lock against current dependency state
safeguard lint [--verbose]Run static-analysis lint passes on all .sc source files
safeguard format [--check]Reindent and whitespace-normalize all .sc/.h source files

check — fast compile-only feedback ​

Like Rust's cargo check: runs every source file through its full front end (for .sc, safec's Preprocessor→Lexer→Parser→Sema→ConstEval — so every type error, borrow-check violation, and region-escape error is still caught; for .c/.cpp, clang -fsyntax-only) but skips assembling object files and skips linking entirely, and never builds the standard library archive — check only needs std/'s headers on the include path, not the linkable implementation. This is normally the majority of build's wall time, so check is the fast inner-loop command for "did I break anything," with build/run reserved for when you actually need a binary.

test — integration tests ​

tests/ is to safeguard test what Rust's tests/ directory is to cargo test: each file is an independent, standalone program with its own main() — not a set of #[test]-annotated functions extracted from one binary, since SafeC has no such attribute. Every file under tests/ is built (linked against the same stdlib and [[dependencies]] as the main project) and run; a test passes if its binary exits 0. This composes naturally with std::test's TestSuite — test_run_and_exit() is designed to be the last line of a test file's main(), translating a suite of assertions into the single pass/fail exit code safeguard test checks:

c
// tests/math_test.sc
#include <std/test/test.h>

void addition_works() {
    std::test_assert_eq_i(2 + 2, 4, "2+2 == 4", "math_test.sc", 4);
}

int main(void) {
    struct TestSuite t = std::TestSuite::new();
    t.add("addition works", addition_works);
    std::test_run_and_exit(&t);   // exits 1 on any failure
}

Why this compiles despite test.h's function-like macros

<std/test/test.h> unconditionally #defines several function-like macros (ASSERT_EQ, ASSERT_TRUE, ...) at the top of the header, and merely including a header containing function-like macro definitions normally fails outside --compat-preprocessor mode ("function-like macros are not allowed in safe mode..."), even in the macro-free calling style shown above. safeguard test specifically compiles every file under tests/ with --compat-preprocessor (unlike build/check, which compile src/ without it) precisely so <std/test/test.h> can be included — verified against a real safeguard test run of the example above.

format — reindenter ​

(safeguard fmt is accepted as a shorter alias.)

Deliberately scoped narrower than a full AST-based pretty-printer like rustfmt or clang-format: it recomputes indentation from {/} nesting depth, trims trailing whitespace, normalizes tabs, and collapses runs of blank lines — but never touches string/comment contents, horizontal spacing within a line, or line-wrapping. This scope was chosen because safec's own Lexer discards comments entirely during tokenization (see Compiler Architecture) — there is no lossless AST for a formatter to round-trip through, so it works from raw source text directly, where safe reindentation is tractable but arbitrary reflow risks corrupting comment/string content. --check reports which files would change without writing them (matching cargo fmt --check / gofmt -l), useful as a CI gate.

lint — static analysis ​

In the spirit of cargo clippy: catches real issues beyond what compilation alone checks. Combines heuristic scans over raw source with safec --dump-ast's own unused-variable warnings. safeguard analyze is accepted as an alias for safeguard lint — both run the identical pass.

CodeLevelDescription
SA000errorSource file could not be opened
SA001warningFile contains more than 5 unsafe {} blocks — consider refactoring
SA002notealloc()/malloc() result is not null-checked on the same line
SA003warningUnused variable (forwarded from safec --dump-ast)
SA004warningEmpty unsafe {} block — has no effect
SA005noteUnresolved TODO/FIXME/XXX marker
SA006warning= instead of == in an if condition
SA007warningDuplicate #include in the same file

Example output ​

src/driver.sc: warning [SA001] file contains 7 unsafe{} blocks — consider refactoring
src/parser.sc:42: note [SA002] result of alloc() should be null-checked
src/parser.sc:58: warning [SA003] warning: unused variable 'tmp'
safeguard: analysis complete — 3 diagnostic(s), 0 error(s)

Returns exit code 0 if no errors (warnings are non-fatal), 1 if any error-level diagnostics are found.

Cross targets ​

--target <alias|triple> (on build, check, test) cross-compiles the project and its standard library for another machine. A bare-metal alias (x86, x86_64, aarch32, aarch64, thumb, thumb2, arm-6m, arm-7m, arm-7em, arm-8m, arm-81m, rv32i, rv32e, rv64i, rv64e, wasm32, wasm64 — see Bare-Metal Targets) implies freestanding mode; any LLVM triple is accepted too.

bash
safeguard build --target arm-7em --release
safeguard test --target rv32e        # builds every test for RV32E, doesn't run them
  • The std archive is built per target under build/deps/<target>/libsafec_std.a, from the std modules the project uses, in the variant for that target (OS-specific backends are skipped on bare metal).
  • Objects — SafeC, C, C++ and Objective-C alike — are compiled with the target's clang flags (safec --print-target-clang-flags), and bare-metal links use ld.lld with -nostdlib -static: supply the linker script, startup code and runtime (memcpy, memset, any malloc, compiler-rt builtins) through [build] cflags/libs.
  • Functions your project defines that freestanding mode would otherwise flag as hosted-only (a runtime's own malloc, say) are passed to the compiler as --provides, so they don't warn.
  • WebAssembly targets link a library module instead: no entry point, exports are the functions marked export_name, unresolved externs become imports, and the std archive includes std/wasm/wasm_rt (the wasm runtime). See WebAssembly.
  • test builds the test binaries without running them (they're for another machine); run refuses a cross target.

Package.toml ​

Every SafeC project has a Package.toml at its root:

toml
[package]
name = "myproject"
version = "0.1.0"

[[dependencies]]
name = "mylib"
version = "https://github.com/user/mylib"

The [package] section defines the project name and version.

Each [[dependencies]] entry names a dependency and where it comes from (see Dependencies).

Dependencies ​

A dependency comes from one of three places:

toml
[[dependencies]]                              # a git repository, cloned to deps/<name>
name    = "mylib"
version = "https://github.com/user/mylib"

[[dependencies]]                              # a local directory
name    = "mylib"
path    = "../mylib"

[[dependencies]]                              # prebuilt library files
name    = "mylib"
lib     = ["vendor/libmylib.a"]               # .a, .so, .dylib or .lib
include = ["vendor/include"]                  # optional header directories

[[dependencies]]                              # a C/C++/ObjC project safeguard builds
name    = "mylib"
path    = "../mylib"                          # or version = "https://..."
build   = "cmake"                             # or "sources"

What a directory provides, whether it's fetched or local, depends on what it contains:

The directory hasIt issafeguard
src/a SafeC packagebuilds src/ (.sc, .c, .cpp) into build/deps/lib<name>.a; include/ and src/ go on the include path
no src/a prebuilt library directorylinks lib<name>.a, lib<name>.so, lib<name>.dylib or <name>.lib from lib/, lib64/ or the directory itself, static first. Without one by that name, it links every library in the first of those that has any (an install with libssl and libcrypto for a dependency named openssl). include/ goes on the include path

A directory whose entry has build is neither: it's an existing C, C++ or Objective-C project that safeguard builds itself (see C/C++ dependencies built from source).

lib names the library files outright and takes precedence over what's in the directory. lib and include paths are relative to the dependency's directory when it has version or path, and to the project root otherwise. A fetched repository can ship prebuilt libraries this way too: version = "https://..." with lib = ["lib/macos-arm64/libmylib.a"]. Shared libraries get an rpath to their directory, so the program finds them at run time. A local path is resolved against the project root. safeguard fetch and build fail with the dependency's name when a library, a directory or an include directory doesn't exist, or when a directory has neither src/ nor a library. Dependency libraries are linked before the standard library, so a SafeC package can use std.

On Windows a DLL is linked through its import library: <name>.lib (or lib<name>.lib) is found like the other names, and the DLL beside it — or in ../bin/, where CMake installs DLLs — is copied next to the program after build, run and test (the job an rpath does elsewhere). lib = ["vendor/mylib.dll"] links the mylib.lib beside it.

C/C++ dependencies built from source ​

A C, C++ or Objective-C library that isn't a safeguard package — a CMake project, or just a directory of sources — can be a dependency built by safeguard itself. build says how; the result goes to build/deps/<name>/:

toml
[[dependencies]]                  # a CMake project
name       = "cppstats"
path       = "../cpplib"          # or version = "https://..." (cloned first)
build      = "cmake"
cmake_args = ["-DCPPSTATS_TESTS=OFF"]

[[dependencies]]                  # a directory of sources
name       = "nslen"
path       = "../nslen"
build      = "sources"
sources    = ["src", "extra/*.c"] # files, directories, '*' patterns
defines    = ["NDEBUG", "LEVEL=2"]
cflags     = ["-fobjc-arc"]
include    = ["include"]          # its public headers
frameworks = ["Foundation"]       # macOS frameworks it needs
buildsafeguard
"sources"compiles the .c/.cpp/.cc/.cxx/.m/.mm files that sources names (default: its src/, recursively, else the files directly in the directory) with defines (-D), cflags and its include directories, into build/deps/<name>/lib<name>.a
"cmake"configures it with the same clang/clang++ the build uses (-G Ninja when ninja is on PATH, Release for --release, Debug otherwise — RelWithDebInfo and MultiThreadedDLL on Windows, the shared release CRT the program uses, since the debug CRT doesn't mix with the program's), plus cmake_args; builds it; installs it into build/deps/<name>/install. The libraries are lib (relative to that install prefix) if given, else lib<name> or every library in its lib/, else the ones in the build tree for a project without install() rules

Headers come from include (relative to the dependency's directory) when it's given; otherwise from include/ — the install's for CMake, the dependency's own for "sources", or the directory itself if it has none. They go on the include path of both SafeC and C/C++ sources.

The build is cached: it reruns only when a file under the dependency's directory or its Package.toml settings changed since the last one. A C++ dependency makes clang++ the link driver (for a CMake one, always — what it compiles can't be told from outside, and clang++ links C just as well); Objective-C adds -lobjc; frameworks are linked on macOS. sources, defines and cflags need build = "sources", cmake_args needs build = "cmake"; anything else is an error naming the dependency. CMake dependencies can't be cross-compiled with --target yet.

SafeC calls these libraries through C declarations, so a C++ library must expose extern "C" functions: C++ classes, templates, overloads and other mangled symbols aren't callable from SafeC. Wrap them in a small C API:

cpp
// cpplib/include/cppstats.h — included by SafeC and C++ alike
#ifdef __cplusplus
extern "C" {
#endif
double cppstats_median(const double* values, int n);
#ifdef __cplusplus
}
#endif
cpp
// cpplib/src/cppstats.cpp
#include "cppstats.h"
#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

extern "C" double cppstats_median(const double* values, int n) {
    std::vector<double> v(values, values + n);
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    return n % 2 ? v[n / 2] : (v[n / 2 - 1] + v[n / 2]) / 2.0;
}
c
// app/src/main.sc
#include <cppstats.h>
extern int printf(const char* fmt, ...);

int main() {
    double samples[5] = { 7.0, 1.0, 4.0, 9.0, 3.0 };
    unsafe { printf("median %.1f\n", cppstats_median(&samples[0], 5)); }
    return 0;
}

The SafeC repository's examples/cpp_dep/ is this project with its CMakeLists.txt, and examples/objc_dep/ an Objective-C one (NSString behind a C API, macOS).

Feature Flags ​

Package.toml can declare a Cargo-style [features] table — named, optional build configurations that gate source code without maintaining separate branches or build scripts:

toml
[features]
default   = ["backend"]              # enabled unless --no-default-features
frontend  = []
backend   = []
fullstack = ["frontend", "backend"]  # enabling one feature can enable others

Each entry's value is a list of other features it also turns on — the same "a feature can pull in other features" model Cargo uses (SafeC has no optional-dependency concept yet, so a feature can only chain other features, not toggle a [[dependencies]] entry on or off).

Select features at build time:

bash
safeguard build                                              # "default" only
safeguard build --features frontend                          # default + frontend
safeguard build --features frontend,backend                  # comma-separated, repeatable
safeguard build --no-default-features --features backend     # backend only

build / check / test / run all accept --features/--no-default-features. safeguard resolves the enabled set (starting from default unless suppressed, following each enabled feature's own sub-feature list to a fixed point) and passes every enabled feature to safec as a preprocessor define:

feature "backend"  ->  -DSAFEC_FEATURE_BACKEND=1
feature "frontend" ->  -DSAFEC_FEATURE_FRONTEND=1

(hyphens in a feature name become underscores). Project source gates on that define with safec's existing preprocessor — no new language syntax:

c
#ifdef SAFEC_FEATURE_BACKEND
#include <std/http/http.h>
#include <std/http/http.h>
// ... server-only code ...
#endif

Feature -D defines apply only to the project's own src//tests/ sources — the standard library and fetched dependencies build the same way regardless of which features the top-level project enabled. All files under src/ are still compiled either way (feature flags decide what code runs, not what gets compiled — an #ifdef'd-out function still exists in the binary as dead code, same as plain C conditional compilation); this keeps the model simple and matches how the rest of safec's preprocessor already works, at the cost of not shrinking binary size or skipping unrelated build errors the way Cargo's per-feature compilation does. See examples/fullstack_demo/ in the SafeC repository for a complete frontend/backend/fullstack project built this way, including a scx frontend (see scx Templating).

Build Flow ​

src/ can freely mix .sc, .c, .cpp/.cc/.cxx, and Objective-C .m/.mm files — each is dispatched by extension and compiled to its own object file independently, never merged into a shared translation unit, so per-file recompilation stays as granular as a pure-SafeC project:

.sc sources          .c / .cpp / .m / .mm sources
    |                       |
safec --emit-llvm      clang / clang++ -c
    |                       |
clang -c ------------> .o files <-----
    |
ar ---------------------> .a static library (for deps)
    |
clang(++) link ----------> executable
  1. Each .sc file is compiled to LLVM IR (.ll) by safec, then assembled to .o by clang -c
  2. Each .c/.cpp/.m/.mm file is compiled straight to .o by clang/clang++ — no LLVM-IR intermediate step, since these are already native compiler front ends
  3. Dependencies are archived into static libraries using ar (also mixed-language aware — a dependency's own src/ can contain .sc/.c/.cpp too)
  4. The final link uses clang++ as the driver whenever any C++ (.cpp or .mm, the project's own or a dependency's) was compiled in (so the C++ runtime — libc++/libstdc++, exceptions, RTTI — links in correctly), plain clang otherwise, and adds -lobjc when there's Objective-C; either way it's linking ordinary object files, since SafeC's C ABI compatibility means a .sc-compiled .o and a .c/.cpp-compiled .o are interchangeable at the object-file level

All three languages share the project's own include/ directory and each dependency's include/ directory for headers — but not SafeC's own std/ directory, which is deliberately kept off the .c/.cpp include path: std/'s headers use #define-based typedefs tuned for SafeC's own preprocessing model, and putting them on a real C/C++ compiler's search path corrupts its own standard headers (e.g. <cstdint>/<vector>) if they happen to shadow the same names.

Example: calling C and C++ from SafeC ​

c
// src/helper.c
int add_c(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
cpp
// src/helper.cpp
#include <vector>
extern "C" int sum_cpp(int a, int b) {
    std::vector<int> v = {a, b};
    int total = 0;
    for (int x : v) total += x;
    return total;
}
c
extern int printf(const char* fmt, ...);
// src/main.sc
extern int add_c(int a, int b);
extern int sum_cpp(int a, int b);

int main() {
    unsafe { printf("%d %d\n", add_c(2, 3), sum_cpp(2, 3)); }
    return 0;
}

A C++ function called from SafeC needs extern "C" on the C++ side (same requirement as calling C++ from plain C) — without it, C++ name mangling means the linker never finds a plain sum_cpp symbol.

Package.toml's [build] srcs = [...] can also list files explicitly (mixed extensions allowed) instead of relying on auto-discovery under src/; cflags = [...] is appended to every clang/clang++ invocation (both .c/.cpp compilation and the final link).

Objective-C ​

.m (Objective-C) and .mm (Objective-C++) files build on macOS; for any other target safeguard stops with an error naming the file. Two [build] keys go with them:

toml
[build]
objc_arc   = true                     # compile .m/.mm with -fobjc-arc
frameworks = ["Cocoa", "Metal"]       # -framework <name> at the final link

frameworks applies to macOS builds only (elsewhere it's dropped with a note). Objective-C classes, like C++ ones, aren't visible to SafeC: give the code a C function to call.

Per-platform settings ​

[build.macos], [build.linux] and [build.windows] take cflags, libs, lib_dirs and frameworks, added to [build]'s own only when building for that OS (the --target's, or the host's) — one manifest can then name each platform's libraries for the project's own code:

toml
[build.macos]
frameworks = ["Security"]

[build.linux]
libs = ["sqlite3"]

[build.windows]
libs = ["winsqlite3", "crypt32"]

The system libraries std's own modules call into (Cocoa, X11 or user32/gdi32 for std::gui, Metal for the GPU backends, ws2_32 for networking on Windows, ...) needn't be listed: safeguard links them for the modules in the build (see Standard Library Modules).

Any other [build.<name>] table, or another key in one, is an error.

C, C++ and Objective-C packages ​

A package needn't contain SafeC at all. safeguard new <name> --lang c (or cpp, objc, objcpp) scaffolds src/main.c (.cpp, .m, .mm; the Objective-C ones with objc_arc = true and frameworks = ["Foundation"]), and such a package builds as a bin, staticlib or cdylib like any other, exporting its headers the same way. When neither the package's sources nor a SafeC source dependency contain SafeC, the standard library is neither built nor linked.

A C, C++ or Objective-C package that calls into std (through extern declarations of its functions, which SafeC exports with C linkage as std_<name>) sets [build] std = true: std is then built and linked, and std's parent directory goes on the C/C++ include path so its headers are reachable as <std/...> (never std/ itself, whose stdint.h and friends would shadow the system's). safeguard new <name> --lang c --std writes that key when the project is created. std = false never links std, even with SafeC sources; std = "all" compiles every std module into the archive, not just the ones the sources include (see Standard Library Modules).

toml
[build]
edition = "2026"
std     = true      # build and link SafeC's std in a C/C++/ObjC package

Linking External Libraries and Library Output ​

Four more [build] keys configure the final link step and what kind of artifact it produces — the same underlying flags safec --emit-bin exposes directly (see Compiler Architecture), here driven by Package.toml instead of the command line:

toml
[build]
libs       = ["m", "pthread"]   # -l<name> at the final link
lib_dirs   = ["/usr/local/lib"] # -L<dir> at the final link
lto        = "thin"             # "" (off, default), "thin", or "full"
crate_type = "bin"              # "bin" (default), "staticlib", or "cdylib"
blas       = "auto"             # CPU BLAS for std's sgemm (see below)

blas picks the CPU vendor's BLAS that sgemm — and through it tensor_matmul and Conv2D::forward — uses, chosen when the program is linked. It is linked only when the build includes std/simd/gemm.h (directly, or through std::ml or std::dsp):

blasLinks
"auto" (default)AOCL-BLAS on AMD CPUs, oneMKL on Intel CPUs, Accelerate on macOS — if the library is found; otherwise none
"aocl" / "mkl" / "openblas" / "accelerate"that library (a warning and std's built-in kernel if it isn't found)
"none"nothing: std's built-in SIMD kernel

Libraries are looked up in AOCL_ROOT, MKLROOT and OPENBLAS_ROOT (or their lib/, lib_LP64/ and lib/intel64/ subdirectories), then in the default install locations (/opt/AMD/aocl/..., /opt/intel/oneapi/mkl/latest/lib). oneMKL is linked with its GNU OpenMP threading layer. SAFEC_BLAS overrides the manifest's choice and SAFEC_BLAS_LIBS replaces the link flags outright. Bare-metal, WebAssembly and Windows builds don't link a BLAS. --verbose prints which one was picked.

crate_type selects what safeguard build produces:

crate_typeOutputHow it's produced
"bin" (default)build/<output>linked executable
"staticlib"build/lib<output>.a and build/include/ar-packed archive of this project's own objects (no linker, no -l/-L/lto — a .a isn't linked, just bundled for a later link to consume)
"cdylib"build/lib<output>.dylib (macOS), build/lib<output>.so (Linux, with that SONAME), or build/<output>.dll and its import library build/<output>.lib (Windows); and build/include/linked with -shared

A library build also exports its public headers to build/include/: everything under the project's include/, and the headers (.h, and C++'s .hh/.hpp/.hxx) under src/, with their paths kept (include/mylib/config.h → build/include/mylib/config.h, src/mylib.h → build/include/mylib.h). These are the headers a dependent building the package from source would see. The directory is rebuilt on every build, so a deleted header leaves it too. A header at the same path in both include/ and src/ is an error. build/ is then a prebuilt dependency as it stands:

toml
[[dependencies]]
name = "mylib"
path = "../mylib/build"    # links libmylib.a, puts build/include on the include path

The project's include/ is on the include path of its own SafeC, C and C++ sources, so a library's sources include the headers it exports the same way its users do.

Windows DLLs ​

A DLL exports only the symbols it's told to, and SafeC has no dllexport. A Windows cdylib therefore exports every external function defined in the package's own object files — the same set a .so or .dylib exposes from them — listed in build/<output>.def (read from the objects with llvm-nm, which ships with LLVM beside clang) and passed to the linker, which also writes the import library build/<output>.lib. Not exported:

  • the standard library's and the dependencies' code linked into the DLL;
  • static functions, and C++-mangled names (SafeC can't call those);
  • global variables — importing data from a DLL needs __declspec(dllimport) on the consumer's side, which SafeC can't express. Export an accessor function instead.

A package that defines no functions gets a warning and no import library. A dependent links <output>.lib and gets the DLL copied beside its executable (Dependencies), so path = "../mylib/build" works on Windows as it does elsewhere.

Every Windows (MSVC-ABI) build uses the shared C runtime: objects are compiled with -fms-runtime-lib=dll (/MD), the link takes msvcrt instead of the static libcmt, and CMake dependencies build with MultiThreadedDLL. A DLL and the program that loads it therefore share one CRT and one heap, so memory allocated on one side of the DLL boundary may be freed on the other, and FILE*s and errno are shared too. The program needs the Universal CRT and the Visual C++ runtime DLLs at run time, which ship with Windows 10 and later (the VC++ redistributable for older systems). MinGW targets keep their own runtime.

safeguard run requires crate_type = "bin" — a static or dynamic library has no executable entry point to run, and running it against the linker directly produces a clear error rather than a confusing OS-level failure.

App Bundles ​

safeguard bundle builds a bin target and packages it the way the platform installs applications. The [bundle] table describes it:

toml
[bundle]
name               = "GuiHello"              # default: the package name
identifier         = "org.example.gui-hello" # required, reverse-DNS
version            = "1.0.0"                 # default: the package version
icon               = "assets/icon.png"       # .png anywhere; .icns (macOS), .ico (Windows)
resources          = ["assets/greeting.txt", "assets/data"]  # files or directories
category           = "Utility"               # freedesktop category, or "public.app-category.*"
copyright          = "Copyright 2026 Example"
subsystem          = "windows"               # Windows: "windows" (default) or "console"
min_system_version = "11.0"                  # macOS LSMinimumSystemVersion (default 11.0)
codesign_identity  = "-"                     # macOS: "-" ad-hoc (default), an identity, "none"
depends            = ["libsqlite3-0"]        # Linux: more of the .deb's Depends
bash
safeguard bundle                              # build/GuiHello.app, build/GuiHello/, or a .deb
safeguard bundle --release --sign "Developer ID Application: Example (TEAMID)"
PlatformOutput
macOSbuild/<name>.app: Contents/MacOS/<output>, Contents/Info.plist (CFBundleIdentifier, CFBundleName, CFBundleExecutable, CFBundleShortVersionString, CFBundleVersion, CFBundleIconFile, NSHighResolutionCapable, LSMinimumSystemVersion, LSApplicationCategoryType), Contents/Resources/ (the icon and the resources) and Contents/Frameworks/ (the dependencies' .dylibs)
Windowsbuild/<name>/: <output>.exe, the dependencies' DLLs and the resources — a portable app folder
Linuxbuild/<pkg>_<version>_<arch>.deb and build/<name>.AppDir

macOS. A .png icon becomes an .icns (scaled to each size with sips, packed with iconutil). Each dependency .dylib copied into Contents/Frameworks gets the install name @rpath/<file> (in the library and in the executable, with install_name_tool), and the executable is linked with an rpath to @executable_path/../Frameworks, so the bundle doesn't depend on the build tree. The nested libraries and then the bundle are signed with codesign: ad-hoc by default, codesign_identity or --sign for a real identity, "none" to skip.

Windows. The executable is linked for the GUI subsystem (/SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS with /ENTRY:mainCRTStartup, so a plain main still works and no console window opens; subsystem = "console" keeps one) with a resource compiled by llvm-rc (or the Windows SDK's rc): the icon (an .ico, or a .png of up to 256×256 wrapped in one), version information from the package (FileVersion, ProductName, CompanyName from the author, ...) and an application manifest declaring per-monitor DPI awareness and Common Controls v6.

Linux. The .deb (built with dpkg-deb) installs /usr/bin/<output>, /usr/share/applications/<identifier>.desktop, the .png icon as /usr/share/icons/hicolor/<w>x<h>/apps/<identifier>.png, the resources under /usr/share/<pkg>/, and the dependencies' shared libraries under /usr/lib/<pkg>/ (on the executable's rpath). DEBIAN/control has Package (the package name in Debian's form, _ becoming -), Version, Architecture (dpkg --print-architecture), Maintainer (the package's author), Description, Installed-Size and Depends: [bundle] depends, plus the packages std's modules name for the system libraries they link (libx11-6 for std::gui on X11). The same tree, with AppRun, the desktop entry and the icon at its top, is build/<name>.AppDir, ready for appimagetool. Without dpkg only the AppDir is made, with a warning.

A GUI program uses std::gui, whose backend calls each platform's own libraries; safeguard links them by itself (Cocoa and the Objective-C runtime, X11, or user32 and gdi32). The SafeC repository's examples/gui_hello/ opens a window, draws for a second and closes it again; its manifest is the [bundle] above, without depends, and names no library.

Standard Library Modules ​

A build compiles and links only the parts of the standard library (std/) it uses — no manual configuration needed — except a package with no SafeC in it, which doesn't use std at all.

Which modules. safeguard reads the #include <std/...> lines of the project's sources (and of the project headers they include, and of a SafeC dependency's sources; with std = true, of its C, C++ and Objective-C sources too). Each std header brings in the std sources implementing it, whose own includes count in turn: std/gui/gui.h brings gui/gui_cocoa.sc on macOS (gui_x11.sc on Linux, gui_win32.sc on Windows), std/ml/tensor.h the tensor core, sgemm and the threading it uses. safeguard test does the same for the files under tests/. Includes inside an #if count, unless the condition is a plain test of __APPLE__, _WIN32 or __linux__ (decided by the target) or, in the project's own files, of a SAFEC_FEATURE_<NAME> macro (decided by its features). The GPU device backends of std::ml come with their features: --features mps builds device_mps.sc, rocm and cuda theirs.

What the code calls. Some of std is called by code no header names: safec compiles new to a call into std/mem.sc, channels (chan_create and the rest) into std/sync/channel.sc, and spawn/join on Linux and macOS into pthread_create/pthread_join. safeguard reads the external symbols of the IR it compiles — the project's sources, a SafeC dependency's, and the std sources in the build — and adds the std sources they call, along with whatever those include and call in turn. A program with no channels and no threads compiles neither sync/channel.sc nor thread.sc, and links no -lpthread on Linux; one using channels gets both, and spawn alone brings thread.sc for -lpthread.

Caching. Each std source compiles to its own object under build/deps/std/ (build/deps/<target>/std/ for a cross target), recompiled only when it, a std header it includes, or the compiler changes; the build's objects are packed into build/deps/libsafec_std.a, from which the linker still takes only what the program references. std is always compiled optimized, with the flags of the prebuilt std (-O2, and on macOS -mmacosx-version-min=11.0 or your MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET), whether the build is a debug or a --release one: the two share these objects, and a debug build doesn't get a slow std. Your own code still follows the build's mode. (Objects compiled before this rule, at -O0, are rebuilt once.) A hello world on std/io.h compiles 4 std sources instead of all 219 (0.4 s instead of 15 s on an M1 Pro), and a program including no std header and calling nothing above, none. A release install compiles none of them at all.

System libraries. The libraries std's modules call into are added to the link — after the objects and archives, deduplicated, and only for the modules in the build:

ModulemacOSLinuxWindows
std/math.h, std/fenv.h-lm-lm(in the C runtime)
std/thread.h, channels, spawn—-lpthread—
std/gui/gui.h-framework Cocoa -lobjc-lX11 (.deb: libx11-6)-luser32 -lgdi32
std/http/http.h, std/sched/——-lws2_32
std/crypto/rng.h——-lbcrypt
std/simd/gemm.h (and std::ml, std::dsp through it)the [build] blas choice: Accelerate by defaultthe [build] blas choice—
std/ml/tensor_vdsp.h, tensor_blas.h-framework Accelerate——
std/ml/gpu_mps.h, --features mps-framework Metal -framework Foundation -lobjc
std/ml/gpu_rocm.h, --features rocm-lamdhip64 -lhiprtc -lrocblas
std/ml/gpu_miopen.h / std/dsp/fft_rocm.h-lMIOpen / -lhipfft
std/ml/gpu_cuda.h, --features cuda-lcuda -lcublas -lcublasLt -lnvrtcthe same
std/ml/gpu_cudnn.h / std/dsp/fft_cuda.h-lcudnn / -lcufftthe same
std/ml/gpu_spirv.h-lvulkan-lvulkan-lvulkan-1
std/ml/gpu_webgpu.h-lwgpu_native-lwgpu_native-lwgpu_native

ROCm's libraries are looked up in $ROCM_PATH/lib (default /opt/rocm/lib), CUDA's in $CUDA_HOME/lib64 (default /usr/local/cuda/lib64; $CUDA_PATH/lib/x64 on Windows), Vulkan's in $VULKAN_SDK, wgpu's in $WGPU_HOME/lib — each added with an rpath when the directory exists. MIOpen and cuDNN stay optional for the device backends (weak references: without them convolutions use im2col + GEMM); a program including gpu_miopen.h or gpu_cudnn.h itself links them. The C library comes with the compiler driver as always. [build] libs/frameworks and [build.<os>] add the project's own libraries after these.

safeguard std-modules prints what a build takes from std — the sources (unit lines) and the system libraries (link, and deb for a .deb's Depends) — for the project, or for std headers and files given on the command line:

bash
$ safeguard std-modules std/gui/gui.h
unit std/atomic.sc
unit std/gui/gui_cocoa.sc
...
link -framework Cocoa
link -lobjc
$ safeguard std-modules --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu std/gui/gui.h
...
link -lX11
deb libx11-6

All of std. [build] std = "all" compiles every std module into the archive, as before modules: for an archive linked by hand (clang prog.ll build/deps/libsafec_std.a ...), or for code that reaches std through extern declarations without including its headers. A staticlib records the std files its sources include in build/lib<output>.a.std, and the symbols its code calls in build/lib<output>.a.refs, so a program linking it as a prebuilt dependency builds those modules too; a library built otherwise needs std = "all" in the program using it.

Writing std. A std header dir/foo.h is implemented by dir/foo.sc and by the dir/foo_<suffix>.sc files that have no header of their own (the platform variants gui_cocoa.sc, fft_f32.sc, ...). Anything else, and the system libraries, is declared in comment lines a std source carries:

c
// safeguard: implements <std/gui/gui.h>        another header this file implements
// safeguard: sources <std/x/extra.sc>          (in a header) another file implementing it
// safeguard: feature mps                       only in builds with this feature
// safeguard: runtime-symbol __safec_chan_      built when the code calls a symbol starting so
// safeguard: runtime baremetal wasm            always built for these targets
// safeguard: link macos -framework Cocoa -lobjc
// safeguard: link linux -L${ROCM_PATH:-/opt/rocm}/lib -lamdhip64
// safeguard: link hosted blas                  the [build] blas choice
// safeguard: deb linux libx11-6

The OS of a link or deb line is macos, linux, windows, bsd, unix (macOS, Linux, BSD), hosted, baremetal, wasm or any. tests/std_modules/check.py, run by CI, compiles every std header alone and fails if a function it declares, or a symbol the modules it brings leave undefined, is defined by a std source outside them.

Each SafeC dependency built from source is similarly compiled to build/deps/lib<name>.a, a C/C++ one into build/deps/<name>/; prebuilt ones are linked from where they are.

Prebuilt std ​

A release archive (and so an install from install.sh/install.ps1) ships std already compiled for its platform, in sections: one archive per top-level directory of std/, and core for the files directly in it.

<prefix>/lib/aarch64-apple-darwin/std/  (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)
├── core.a            std/*.sc: io, fmt, mem, string, math, thread, ...
├── core.units        its stamp (the safec that built it, a hash of the binary, and
│                     the target), each source's input hash and the symbols it calls
├── collections.a     std/collections/
├── collections.units
├── gui.a, gui.units
├── ml.a, ml.units
└── ...               alloc, crypto, debug, dsp, encoding, fs, hal, http, interrupt,
                      ipc, kernel, net, reactive, rpc, sched, scx, serial, simd, sync, test

Each archive holds the section's sources that no feature gates, compiled optimized as above (for macOS 11.0 and later on macOS). A native build looks for the sections beside the safec it uses (<bin>/../lib/<triple>/std/) and under $SAFEC_HOME/lib/<triple>/std/. The modules are worked out as above; then each one comes from its section when that section is installed and its stamp matches the compiler and the host, and is compiled otherwise. The build links only the sections holding its modules: a hello world on std/io.h and std/collections/vec.h links core.a and collections.a, not gui.a or ml.a, and compiles no std at all; nor does a std::gui window or a std::ml training loop.

What a section doesn't have is compiled into build/deps/libsafec_std.a:

  • a section that isn't installed (install.sh --std=..., see below): its sources the build uses are compiled, the other sections still linked prebuilt;
  • a GPU backend whose feature is on (--features mps, ...);
  • a std source changed since the release was built: it is compiled, and the section is linked from a copy without its old object (build/deps/std-prebuilt/<section>.a), so no source is linked twice.

--verbose says which sections are linked and which sources are compiled and why:

safeguard: std modules (6): atomic.sc collections/vec.sc io.sc io_file.sc mem.sc panic.sc
safeguard: std section 'collections' is not installed in ~/safec/lib/aarch64-apple-darwin/std; compiling its units from source: std/collections/vec.sc
safeguard: linking the prebuilt std sections core from ~/safec/lib/aarch64-apple-darwin/std

Cross, bare-metal and WebAssembly builds don't use the prebuilt std; neither does a build with [build] std_prebuilt = false, SAFEC_STD_FROM_SOURCE=1 or extra compiler flags, or, on macOS, with a MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET older than 11.0. A section stamped for another compiler or target is passed over and compiled from source, with a note under --verbose. On macOS the sections are built for 11.0, so a program built for 11.0 or later links them without "built for newer macOS version" warnings; safeguard passes no minimum of its own, and clang's default (the running macOS) or MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET applies to your code.

Choosing sections. install.sh --std=core,collections,gui installs only those sections (install.ps1 -Std core,collections,gui); the default is all. --std=+ml (-Std +ml) adds sections to an existing install later, from the release it was installed from (recorded in <prefix>/.release), changing nothing else. std's sources are always installed, so any section works either way; a missing one only costs its compile time, once per project.

safeguard std-prebuilt <prefix> writes the sections (the release workflow runs it through .github/scripts/package.sh, which lays out the whole install). tests/std_modules/check.py --prebuilt <prefix>/lib/<triple>/std checks them: each section holds exactly its sources, no symbol is defined in two sections, and each std header's modules are complete with only their sections linked.

SAFEC_STD_ARCHIVE=/path/to/libsafec_std.a links that archive instead, whatever it is: nothing is compiled, the linker takes the members the program references, and the system libraries still come from the modules the sources include when std/ is found (SAFEC_HOME). Without std/, safeguard can't tell which modules are used and adds none: list them in [build] libs/frameworks.

Environment Setup ​

safeguard locates the SafeC toolchain using the SAFEC_HOME environment variable:

bash
export SAFEC_HOME=/path/to/SafeC

This should point to the SafeC repository root. From there, safeguard auto-discovers:

  • The safec compiler binary at $SAFEC_HOME/compiler/build/safec
  • The standard library at $SAFEC_HOME/std/
  • In an install, the prebuilt std sections at $SAFEC_HOME/lib/<triple>/std/

Project Structure ​

A typical SafeC project created with safeguard new:

myproject/
├── Package.toml
├── src/
│   └── main.sc
└── build/           (created by safeguard build)
    ├── deps/
    │   ├── libsafec_std.a
    │   └── lib<dep>.a
    └── myproject    (final executable)

Example Workflow ​

bash
# Create a new project
safeguard new hello

# Enter the project directory
cd hello

# Edit src/main.sc
# ...

# Build and run
safeguard run

# Or build separately
safeguard build --release
./build/hello

Reproducible Builds ​

After every successful build, safeguard writes a Package.lock file that pins:

  • The safec compiler binary (FNV-1a 64-bit hash)
  • Each dependency's git commit SHA (git rev-parse HEAD)
  • Each source file's content hash
toml
[safec]
hash = "a3f5c8d2e1b04976"

[dep.mylib]
url     = "https://github.com/user/mylib"
git_sha = "c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2"

[sources]
"src/main.sc"   = "9f8e7d6c5b4a3f2e"
"src/utils.sc"  = "1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b"

Verifying a lock ​

bash
safeguard verify-lock

Checks that each dependency's current HEAD matches the locked SHA. If any dependency has drifted, the command prints a warning and exits with code 1. When the compiler binary hash changes, a warning is printed but the build is not blocked.

Blocking builds on drift ​

safeguard build automatically calls checkLock() before compiling. A dependency SHA mismatch is a hard error that aborts the build (a safec binary hash mismatch, by contrast, only warns — see above):

safeguard: error: dependency 'mylib' git SHA mismatch (locked=c3d4e5f... current=a1b2c3d...)
  Run 'safeguard fetch' to update, then rebuild.

Building safeguard ​

The package manager itself is built with CMake:

bash
cd safeguard
cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build

The resulting binary is build/safeguard.
